titre: The Nasadiya Hymn: A Creation Song That Ends on a Question
accroche: In the Rig-Veda, hymn 10.129 tells of the beginning of the world, then wonders whether even the one who looks down from on high knows it.
contenu_vulgarise:
We expect an account of origins to know. A god creates, a chaos separates, a word brings forth light: the account holds together through the assurance of its narrator. In the Rig-Veda, the oldest collection of Sanskrit texts, one hymn does otherwise. The tenth book counts 191; the 129th, of only seven stanzas, is one of the most quoted in all of Indian literature, and it begins by denying that there was a beginning that can be described.

## Seven Stanzas

The hymn is known by its first word, nāsadāsīt, “there was no non-being.” In Ralph Griffith's English translation (1889), the first stanza says that then there existed neither the existent nor the non-existent, neither the air nor the sky beyond. Nothing distinguished day from night. Something breathed without breath, by its own nature; apart from it, there was nothing. Then comes heat, and desire (kāma), described as the first seed of the mind. The sages, searching in their hearts, find the link between being and non-being.

What follows turns against the author himself. Who really knows, who can say where this creation came from? The gods, the hymn adds, came afterward: they cannot therefore bear witness to it. And the last stanza posits the only one who could know, he who has watched over this world from the highest heaven, then the hymn leaves the sentence open: he knows it, or perhaps he does not.

## What the Doubt Says, and What It Does Not

The hymn is sometimes presented as an “agnostic” or “skeptical” text. The formula is tempting, because it makes the ancient world heard in the words of ours. It goes a bit fast: the hymn denies no god, and the Indian tradition has read it in very different ways, as a text of metaphysics, of cosmological speculation, or of the poetry of mystery. What is established is its form: a sacred poem that, at the point where one expects revelation, poses a question, and does not close it.

This detail shifts a common idea about foundational texts. We imagine them uniform: a sacred book speaks with a single voice, with authority. The Rig-Veda contains, within its own pages, a song that questions the authority of its gods. The uncertainty is written into the collection itself, not added by a modern commentator.

repere.texte: The Nasadiya hymn (Rig-Veda 10.129) has seven stanzas. In Ralph T. H. Griffith's translation (1889), the seventh leaves open the question of whether the one who watches over the world from the highest heaven knows the origin of creation: “he verily knows it, or perhaps he knows not.”
repere.source: Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Rigveda, Benares, 2nd ed., 1897, book 10, hymn 129; transcription at creationmyths.org

carte.punch: A sacred hymn of India tells of the creation of the world, and ends on “perhaps he knows not.”
carte.idee: Rig-Veda 10.129 has seven stanzas on the origin of the world. It says that even the gods came afterward, then leaves open whether the one who watches from on high knows it. A sacred text that carries its own doubt.

quiz.question: How does the Nasadiya hymn (Rig-Veda 10.129) conclude its account of creation?
choix: By naming a single creator god, identified in the last stanza
By the question, left open, of whether the one who watches over the world really knows where it came from
By a description of the end of the world, answering the beginning
By a prohibition on humans trying to understand the origin
quiz.explication: The hymn identifies no creator, describes no end of the world, and prescribes no prohibition: the last stanza leaves open whether the one who watches from on high knows or not. Readings of this doubt vary, but the open form is in the text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Nasadiya hymn describe as the first seed of the mind, after the coming of heat?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The hymn says that heat comes, then desire (kāma), described as the first seed of the mind; the sages only afterward search in their hearts for the link between being and non-being.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does the Nasadiya hymn state that the gods cannot bear witness to the origin of creation?
choix: Because they swore to keep silent on this subject
Because they themselves came after the creation
Because they lost the memory of this event
Because they lived too far from the place of creation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The hymn explicitly says that the gods came after the creation: they therefore cannot bear witness to it, which has nothing to do with an oath, a loss of memory, or geographic distance.
